## Vineyard versus vineyard module

For a fixed complex $K$ with changing filtration function
$f_t:K\to\mathbb R$, a vineyard records trajectories of persistence-diagram
points. A vineyard module retains the persistence module $V_t$ at each
external time together with coherent maps between modules at different times.
Schematically,

$$
\begin{array}{ccccc}
V_s(a)&\longrightarrow&V_s(b)&\longrightarrow&V_s(c)\\
\downarrow&&\downarrow&&\downarrow\\
V_t(a+\varepsilon)&\longrightarrow&V_t(b+\varepsilon)&\longrightarrow&V_t(c+\varepsilon).
\end{array}
$$

Barcodes classify suitable individual one-parameter modules, but source and
target barcodes do not classify a particular map between them. Dynamic
questions may depend on those missing maps.

## The Turner teaching example

Turner's example divides a disc into four pieces [@turner2023vineyard]:

- $A$: open inner disc;
- $B$: inner boundary circle;
- $C$: open surrounding annulus; and
- $D$: outer boundary circle.

Assign

$$
f_t(A)=21-t,\qquad f_t(B)=14-t,\qquad
f_t(C)=15+t,\qquad f_t(D)=t.
$$

The horizontal direction is external time $t$ and the vertical direction is
filtration height. At a fixed $t$, moving vertically reveals the sublevel-set
filtration. Critical orderings change at

$$f_3(A)=f_3(C),\qquad f_7(B)=f_7(D).$$

At each time there are two $H_1$ intervals,

$$[14-t,21-t),\qquad[t,15+t).$$

Following their endpoints through time produces two visible vines.

## Why two vines need not be independent

Before the critical events, use the basis

$$[B],\qquad[D+B],$$

while later the forced basis is

$$[B],\qquad[D].$$

Over $\mathbb F_2$,

$$[D]=[D+B]+[B].$$

The change mixes the two visible directions. After coherent simplification,
an off-diagonal term remains:

$$
T=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.
$$

The off-diagonal $1$ says that transporting the second generator necessarily
acquires a contribution from the first in these bases. There is no globally
coherent basis that separates the family into two independent one-dimensional
problems. The vineyard module is therefore indecomposable even though the
vineyard visibly contains two vines.

::: {.callout-note title="What to retain if the algebra is skipped"}
A vineyard shows trajectories of interval endpoints. It does not determine
every linear relation between the underlying homology generators. The matrix
calculation is one concrete demonstration of that information gap.
:::

## Why this is delicate for moving point clouds

Smooth point motion need not produce a gently changing Rips filtration order.
Many edge lengths can cross simultaneously, changing triangles and
higher-dimensional simplices. Diagram stability does not imply stable feature
identity:

$$
\text{diagram stability}\neq\text{reliable feature tracking}.
$$

A fixed mesh carrying a smooth field, or a fixed interaction scaffold with
changing weights, is often a more plausible vineyard domain than the literal
Rips filtration of moving agents.
